  3124. forward passes to replace sequential rollout, however their approach doubles the input length (as well as KV cache
  3125. size) so they introduce more training and inference overhead than the full bandwidth transformer.
  3126. Parallel training of recurrent networks. Another related direction is parallel training of recurrent networks.
  3127. Most applications of this consider the linear special case like Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2024) or Gated Deltanet (Yang
  3128. et al., 2025). These are clearly powerful techniques with use in various architectures yet in all such uses they
  3129. are hybridized with standard transformer layers which can compensate for the missing representational capacity
  3130. inherited from the linear constraint. ParaRNN (Danieli et al., 2025) goes further by parallelizing training of
  3131. nonlinear recurrent neural networks via decoupling the optimizations at each point in the process and using
  3132. newton’s iterations to achieve convergence with results comparable to transformers for language modeling. This
  3133. approach here goes the other way, constructing recurrence on transformers with results that improve over baseline
  3134. transformers, and it appears that the approach here is significantly more efficient.
  3135. Data-efficient pre-training. Lastly, our work falls into the broad category of improving LLM pre-training’s data
  3136. efficiency, i.e., given the same model size and fixed data, how can we use more flops to build a more powerful
  3137. model under fixed or more inference overhead. Existing approaches consider additional objectives (beyond NTP)
  3138. on the representation (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Dai et al., 2025; Teoh et al., 2025) that encourage
  3139. the hidden state to contain richer information. There has also been a recent NanoGPT slow run competition
  3140. 2
  3141. that
  3142. studies this setting, where the official solution (Mandal et al., 2026) trains a deep ensemble of LLMs and distills
  3143. them into a single one for better performance. Compared with these approaches, our framework uses additional
  3144. training flops for unlocking a new type of decoding regime that gives a free performance boost at inference time.
  3145. Additionally, we believe techniques can flow between literature, for example, the depth scaling we used has also
  3146. been shown to be important for the stability of training loop transformers (Movahedi et al., 2026). Our empirical
  3147. verification of recurrence scheduling also suggests the feasibility of introducing computationally intensive auxiliary
  3148. objectives only later on in the training.
  3149. Loop transformers (Fan et al., 2026; Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Geiping et al., 2025) also fall into
  3150. this category, where additional training FLOPs enable test-time scaling through repeated computation at inference.
  3151. Our approach is similar to loop transformers during training in that the model’s outputs are repeatedly fed back
  3152. as inputs across multiple forward passes. At inference time, however, the two approaches differ in where the
  3153. additional computation is paid. Loop transformers obtain additional effective depth by explicitly reapplying the
  3154. transformer stack, thereby increasing inference compute with the number of recurrent steps. In contrast, latent
  3155. feedback is integrated into the autoregressive decoding loop: it reuses the top-layer state already produced at the
  3156. previous token and requires only a lightweight fusion operation, without additional transformer-block evaluations
  3157. per generated token. Thus, full-bandwidth transformers retain much of the benefit of recurrent computation while
  3158. incurring negligible per-token decoding overhead, with additional compute required only when optional multi-pass
  3159. prefilling is used.
  3160. More broadly, these methods point to a shift in the relevant scaling axes for pre-training. Conventional scaling
  3161. primarily varies model parameters and training tokens. However, in large-scale training, the feasible design space is
  3162. also constrained by pod size of GPUs, wall-clock budget, and the availability of high-quality unique tokens. Once
  3163. the token-per-parameter ratio and the accessible pool of high-quality data become binding, simply increasing the
  3164. number of unique training tokens is no longer the only, or even the most direct, path to improvement. A promising
  3165. axis is to spend more computation per unique token through recurrent, iterative, or feedback-based mechanisms.
  3166. 6 Limitation
  3167. There are two major limitations of the current work. Firstly our experiment scale is limited to 1B parameter models,
  3168. and we did not verify the approach on models of larger scale. However we believe latent feedback decoding
  3169. can potentially introduce more benefit for a deeper model where the top layer hidden state includes even richer
  3170. information. Secondly, the feedback pass scheduling is based on a heuristic; future work can consider more rigorous
  3171. ablation on the length of the recurrence training phase as well as more principled approach to determine the number
  3172. of recurrence steps, e.g. via the Jacobi iteration convergence diagnostics from Zeng et al. (2025).

  3295. Full-bandwidth transformer
  3296. A Model architecture
  3297. The model is a decoder-only causal language model with a tied 100,352-token embedding and output head, 24
  3298. transformer layers, a 1,536-dimensional hidden state, and 6,656-dimensional SiLU GLU feed-forward blocks.
  3299. Its gated grouped-query attention uses 16 query heads, 8 shared key/value heads, headwise gates, QK RMS
  3300. normalization, and rotary positions over an 8,192-token context; most layers use a 2,048-token sliding window,
  3301. while every sixth layer uses full attention. RMS normalization is applied around each residual block and at the final
  3302. output.

  3343. The implementation on vLLM follows the same design pattern as EAGLE Li et al. (2024a) / MTP Gloeckle et al.
  3344. (2024): it retains each request’s latest trunk hidden state and copies it in place into a persistent, fixed-address
  3345. model buffer before the next decode step, allowing CUDA graphs to capture the glu cross gate (Eq. (4)) inside
  3346. forward. A patched GPUModelRunner._model_forward stores detached hidden states in a dictionary
  3347. keyed by request ID, uses query_start_loc to map packed rows to requests, and removes completed requests.

  3376. We construct paired synthetic examples whose label is determined by information appearing before a shared final
  3377. colon. The target token itself is never included in the input. We append 0, 8, 32, 128, or 256 semantically null
  3378. scratch updates, allowing us to vary sequence length without changing the target. At the final colon, we record the
  3379. layer-0 input and the output of every Transformer block.
  3380. Completion tracking. Each input specifies a required count a and a completed count b. The target is DONE
  3381. if a = b and MORE otherwise. For each unordered numeral pair {a, b}, we include all four assignments
  3382. (a, a), (a, b), (b, a), (b, b), balancing every numeral across fields and labels. A representative matched pair, abbrevi-
  3383. ated to show eight repeated distractors, is
  3384. required = 4 required = 4
  3385. completed = 9 completed = 4
  3386. scratch = 7 scratch = 7
  3387. scratch += 0 scratch += 0
  3388. ... (8 updates) ... (8 updates)

  3890. <div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
  3891.    
  3892. <p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full-bandwidth transformer</em>, which widens this channel with <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent feedback</em>: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.</p>
  3893.  
  3894. </div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span><sup id="footnotex1.1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>Correspondence to Xi Wang

John Langford <<a href="mailto:jcl@microsoft.com" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">jcl@microsoft.com</a>>. <math id="footnotex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math> Work done during an internship at Microsoft AI Frontiers.

  3898. <section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
  3899. <h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>
  3900.  
  3901. <div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3902. <p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scaling large language models has largely meant increasing model parameters and training on more tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>)</cite>. As pre-training continues to scale, however, the availability of high-quality unique data becomes an increasingly constraint. This motivates revisiting the scaling axes themselves: rather than relying solely on more data, can we extract more useful learning signal from each token by allocating more computation to it? Recurrent, iterative, and feedback-based computation offer a natural way to pursue this direction, but additional FLOPs matter only if they translate into richer representations during training or more effective computation at inference time.</p>
  3903. </div>
  3904. <div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3905. <p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Autoregressive transformers expose a particularly underused opportunity for such computation. They already contain a feedback loop: the token sampled at step <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-1</annotation></semantics></math> becomes the input at step <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, left).
  3906. This loop is what lets chain-of-thought decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>)</cite> perform computation whose depth grows with the number of generated tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>)</cite>.
  3907. But measured as a communication channel, the loop is extremely narrow:
  3908. Decoding compresses the model’s entire top-layer state, a <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional vector, down to a single symbol carrying at most <math id="S1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log_{2}|V|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_{2}|V|</annotation></semantics></math> bits.
  3909. Non-verbalized computation is not erased—intermediate activations persist in the KV cache and remain accessible—but it is <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">depth-frozen</em>: a state produced at layer <math id="S1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is readable only by layers above <math id="S1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, so it can never return to the bottom of the stack for further processing, and the deepest state of all, the top layer’s output, is never cached. Verbalization is thus the only channel by which information re-enters the bottom layer and receives fresh computation, at the cost of being squeezed through a single token. The model must either spend tokens narrating its intermediate state or recompute that state from scratch at every position.</p>
  3910. </div>
  3911. <div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3912. <p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full-bandwidth transformer</em> where we widen this channel to its full width.
  3913. In particular, we introduce latent feedback decoding, which fuses the previous top-layer hidden state with the sampled token’s embedding during decoding, through a gated linear unit using the state on the value pathway, the token acting as the gate, and feeds the result back as the next input (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> right, Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>).
  3914. We call a transformer capable of decoding this way a full-bandwidth transformer, since its inter-step feedback now carries the entire hidden state rather than a thin token.
  3915. The sampled token is retained, so the model still produces ordinary text and can be flexibly trained with standard supervised language modeling losses; what changes is that the feedback is no longer limited to the token’s identity.
  3916. By design, this affords two things standard decoding lacks: (i) non-verbalized state—uncertainty, partial results, plans—can re-enter the bottom of the stack with a renewed depth budget and be processed further across steps, rather than staying frozen in the cache at the level where it was produced; (ii) every layer, including the shallowest, sees the past as processed by the <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full</em> stack, not only by the layers beneath it;
  3917. Crucially, these come with almost no architecture changes and extra serving cost: the fusion adds two matrix multiplications per generated token, attention and the KV cache are untouched, and prefill is run either once or, optionally, twice for better performance.</p>
  3918. </div>
  3919. <div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3920. <p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The obstacle is training. A pretrained model has never seen hidden states in its input, so latent feedback cannot simply be switched on at inference; and the recurrence it defines is sequential over positions, so training on it directly would forfeit the parallel teacher forcing that makes transformers efficient to train.
  3921. We resolve this with a <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">multi-pass</em> regime (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Parallel training for latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>): each pass shifts the previous pass’s hidden states one position rightward, fuses them with the token embeddings, and re-runs the stack in parallel across all positions, so sequentiality is paid across a handful of passes rather than across the sequence.
  3922. Two ingredients make this practical. A <em id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">progressive schedule</em> spends the bulk of training on the ordinary single-pass objective such that the run can start from a standard pretraining checkpoint and introduces extra feedback passes only late; and a <em id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">prefix mixin</em> randomizes where fused inputs begin within a sequence, matching the prompt-then-generate structure of inference.
  3923. Empirically, we find the schedule’s composition matters in an unexpected way: training with two feedback passes alone produces a recurrence that <em id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diverges</em> once rolled past its trained depth, whereas mixing in as little as 3% three-pass batches turns the learned map into a <em id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">contraction</em> toward a fixed point that stays stable beyond the trained depth (Fig. <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3 Parallel training for latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
  3924. </div>
  3925. <div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3926. <p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Empirically, full-bandwidth transformers convert negligible extra inference compute into gains equivalent to substantially more training data.
  3927. Utilizing multiple forward pass for prefill, the recurrence-trained model matches no-recurrence baselines trained on twice the tokens in both validation loss and multiple-choice accuracy (Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Fused prefilling improves non-generative performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
  3928. On free-form generation (Fig. <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2 Latent feedback decoding improves decoding performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>)—GSM8K, Math500, HumanEval, MBPP—latent feedback improves over standard decoding of the <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">same</em> weights on every task, matches the <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math>-token baselines, and on some tasks approaches baselines trained with up to <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math> the tokens; the gains carry over through long-context extension and instruction tuning (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ The improvement carries over through instruction tuning. ‣ 4.2 Latent feedback decoding improves decoding performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
  3929. On base models, latent feedback often yields markedly shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy (Fig. <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ The improvement carries over through instruction tuning. ‣ 4.2 Latent feedback decoding improves decoding performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.4 Full-bandwidth transformer carries richer information in shallow-layer residuals ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>)—the behavior the widened channel predicts, with computation riding the hidden state instead of being verbalized token by token.</p>
  3930. </div>
  3931. <figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2608.08888v1/figures/fig1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" width="616" height="319" alt="Refer to caption">
  3932. <figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
  3933. <span id="S1.F1.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Standard decoding vs. latent feedback decoding.</span>
  3934. <span id="S1.F1.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left</span>: In a standard transformer, the current state can access only lower-layer past states (blue); deeper past states (white) are unreachable, and the only inter-step feedback is the sampled token embedding (green).
  3935. <span id="S1.F1.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right</span>: A <em id="S1.F1.9.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">full-bandwidth transformer</em> uses <em id="S1.F1.9.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">latent feedback</em>, fusing the previous top-layer hidden state with the sampled token embedding through a dimension-preserving gate (<math id="S1.F1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\otimes" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\otimes</annotation></semantics></math>, Eq. (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.1 Latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>)) and feeding it back as the next input. This returns full hidden-state information to the bottom of the stack, making the past as processed by all layers accessible to subsequent computation.
  3936. </span></figcaption>
  3937. </figure>
  3938. </section>
  3939. <section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
  3940. <h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>
  3941.  
  3942. <div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3943. <p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a vocabulary of size <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|V|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|V|</annotation></semantics></math> and a <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional residual stream, a decoder-only LLM maps an input sequence of <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, with embeddings <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\bm{e}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\bm{e}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>, through <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> attention–MLP blocks. The final-layer hidden states <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\bm{h}_{t}^{L}\}_{t=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\bm{h}_{t}^{L}\}_{t=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> are projected by the language-model head <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{\text{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mtext>head</mtext></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>V</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{\text{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times D}</annotation></semantics></math> to next-token distributions:</p>

  3953. <section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
  3954. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">KV cache.</h4>
  3955.  
  3956. <div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3957. <p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">During autoregressive decoding with transformers, previously computed keys and values are cached and reused, avoiding repeated computation over the prefix. Unlike RNNs and state-space models, which compress history into a fixed-size recurrent state, dense-attention transformers retain explicit representations of all past tokens, so each new hidden state can attend directly to the full cached history.</p>
  3958. </div>
  3959. </section>
  3960. <section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
  3961. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bandwidths of a model’s horizonal axis vs. veritical axis.</h4>
  3962.  
  3963. <div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3964. <p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">It is useful to separate the horizontal axis (across positions) from the vertical axis (across depth), because the two carry information at different rates. <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Horizontally</em>, dense attention is effectively full-bandwidth: when generating token <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the layer-<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> state <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}_{t}^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t}^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> can read the cached representations of every earlier position. <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Vertically</em>, access is restricted: <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}_{t}^{\ell}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t}^{\ell}</annotation></semantics></math> cannot read any deeper past state <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}_{t^{\prime}}^{\ell^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>?</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t^{\prime}}^{\ell^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t^{\prime}<t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo><</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t^{\prime}<t</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\prime}\geq\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>≥</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\prime}\geq\ell</annotation></semantics></math> (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, left). Formally, the states reachable when computing position <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> at layer <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> are</p>
  3965. <table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  3966.  
  3967. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  3968. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  3969. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{R}_{\text{std}}(t,\ell)=\big\{(t^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}):t^{\prime}<t,\;\ell^{\prime}<\ell\big\},\qquad\bigl\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{std}}\bigr\rvert=\Theta(T\ell)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mtext>std</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo><</mo><mi>t</mi><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo><</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>std</mi></msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}_{\text{std}}(t,\ell)=\big\{(t^{\prime},\ell^{\prime}):t^{\prime}<t,\;\ell^{\prime}<\ell\big\},\qquad\bigl\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{std}}\bigr\rvert=\Theta(T\ell),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  3970. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  3971. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  3972. </table>
  3973. <p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">so a shallow layer of a new token sees only a <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">partially processed</em> view of the past, even though the deeper, more fully processed states of those same positions have already been computed and sit in the cache.
  3974. Past computation therefore persists but is <em id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">depth-frozen</em> in that the representations produced at layer <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> is readable only to layers above <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell</annotation></semantics></math> and can never be routed back down for further processing. This is the narrow vertical channel that sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a> widens.</p>
  3975. </div>
  3976. <div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3977. <p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, this depth-wise dependency constraint is also what lets transformers train in parallel across positions: sequential computation is required only across layers, not across tokens. At decoding time, however, generation is already sequential over tokens, so the constraint buys nothing—opening the door to richer dependencies on past hidden states, which we develop next.</p>
  3978. </div>
  3979. </section>
  3980. </section>
  3981. <section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
  3982. <h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding</h2>
  3983.  
  3984. <section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
  3985. <h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Latent feedback decoding</h3>
  3986.  
  3987. <div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  3988. <p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The central innovation in full-bandwidth transformer is latent feedback decoding, which feeds the previous top-layer hidden state back into the input. At step <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
  3989. <table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  3990.  
  3991. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  3992. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  3993. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{h}_{t}^{L}=f_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{e}_{t}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L};\;C\right),\qquad\textrm{where}~\bm{e}_{t}\leftarrow\mathrm{Decode}\!\left(\bm{W}^{\textrm{head}}\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L}\right),\;C=\bm{e}_{0},\bm{e}_{1}\otimes\bm{h}_{0}^{L},\ldots,\bm{e}_{t-1}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-2}^{L}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.447em">;</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mtext>where</mtext><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mpadded style="width:3.055em;" width="3.055em"><mi>Decode</mi></mpadded><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>?</mi><mtext>head</mtext></msup><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.447em">,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mn>0</mn><mi>L</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t}^{L}=f_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{e}_{t}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L};\;C\right),\qquad\textrm{where}~\bm{e}_{t}\leftarrow\mathrm{Decode}\!\left(\bm{W}^{\textrm{head}}\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L}\right),\;C=\bm{e}_{0},\bm{e}_{1}\otimes\bm{h}_{0}^{L},\ldots,\bm{e}_{t-1}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-2}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  3994. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  3995. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  3996. </table>
  3997. <p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-layer transformer stack, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\cdot\otimes\cdot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⊗</mo><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cdot\otimes\cdot</annotation></semantics></math> fuses the sampled token’s embedding with the previous latent state, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> is the past context (the KV cache of all earlier positions). Standard decoding (Eq. (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>)) is the special case in which only the sampled token crosses between steps.</p>
  3998. </div>
  3999. <div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4000. <p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The fusion <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\otimes" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\otimes</annotation></semantics></math> is a gated linear unit:</p>
  4001. <table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  4002.  
  4003. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  4004. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  4005. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{e}_{t}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-1}=\bm{W}^{U}\bm{h}_{t-1}\odot\sigma(\bm{W}^{G}\bm{e}_{t})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>?</mi><mi>U</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>?</mi><mi>G</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{e}_{t}\otimes\bm{h}_{t-1}=\bm{W}^{U}\bm{h}_{t-1}\odot\sigma(\bm{W}^{G}\bm{e}_{t}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  4006. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  4007. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  4008. </table>
  4009. <p id="S3.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{W}^{U},\bm{W}^{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>?</mi><mi>U</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>?</mi><mi>G</mi></msup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{W}^{U},\bm{W}^{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}</annotation></semantics></math>. The asymmetry is deliberate: the hidden state occupies the value pathway, while the token embedding enters only as a multiplicative gate. A symmetric fusion such as <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{e}_{t}+\bm{W}\bm{h}_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>?</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{e}_{t}+\bm{W}\bm{h}_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> would leave a shortcut open: the model could suppress the state pathway, recover the plain token input, and reach ordinary pretraining loss, leaving the wide channel unused. That shortcut is especially tempting when training starts from a standard checkpoint whose low loss the additive path can reproduce. Eq. (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.1 Latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) closes it, since discarding <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> discards the input itself, and the token’s identity survives only in the <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional gating pattern it imposes on the state. Reading the state is thereby mandatory rather than optional.</p>
  4010. </div>
  4011. <section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
  4012. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent feedback is free to serve.</h4>
  4013.  
  4014. <div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4015. <p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The added inference cost is independent of context-length and model-depth and under <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\%</annotation></semantics></math> per token. The state <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is already computed during standard decoding, so the only extra work is the fusion: two <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\times D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\times D</annotation></semantics></math> matrix multiplications, negligible against a forward pass through <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> blocks. Because fusion preserves the input dimension <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, the architecture, KV-cache layout, and serving stack are untouched, and the decoding loop changes by two lines (Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3 Parallel training for latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, right). The scheme is also vLLM-compatible: we store top-layer states in a dedicated buffer, adapting the mechanism used by multi-token-prediction implementations (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D vLLM compatibility ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>).</p>
  4016. </div>
  4017. </section>
  4018. </section>
  4019. <section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
  4020. <h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Latent feedback decoding vs. standard CoT</h3>
  4021.  
  4022. <div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4023. <p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard CoT performs serial computation through a single feedback channel: each token is appended to the context and becomes the next input. The state is the token sequence,</p>
  4024. <table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  4025.  
  4026. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  4027. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  4028. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="s_{t+1}=s_{t}\|a_{t},\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\in\mathcal{V},\qquad s_{t}=x_{1:t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">?</mi><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t+1}=s_{t}\|a_{t},\qquad a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\in\mathcal{V},\qquad s_{t}=x_{1:t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  4029. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  4030. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  4031. </table>
  4032. <p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">so the only thing crossing between steps is the discrete action sequence.
  4033. The underlying problem-solving state may in principle be a deterministic function of the past actions, but recovering it from the token history is itself a state-tracking problem, and a fixed-depth transformer has only bounded serial computation per forward pass. CoT sidesteps this by externalizing intermediate state into language: the model writes out partial results, subgoals, and bookkeeping, then conditions future computation on the written trace.</p>
  4034. </div>
  4035. <div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4036. <p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{i}=\bm{e}(a_{i-1})\otimes\bm{z}_{i-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>?</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{i}=\bm{e}(a_{i-1})\otimes\bm{z}_{i-1}</annotation></semantics></math> be the fused input at position <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>
  4037. (with <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{u}_{1}=\bm{e}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>?</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{1}=\bm{e}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>), so the attended context is <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="C_{t}=\bm{u}_{1:t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>?</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{t}=\bm{u}_{1:t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.
  4038. The state is <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="s_{t}=(a_{1:t},\,\bm{z}_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}=(a_{1:t},\,\bm{z}_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>: the token trace and the most recent
  4039. latent. One step for latent feedback decoding is</p>
  4040. <table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  4041.  
  4042. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  4043. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  4044. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\in\mathcal{V},\qquad\bm{z}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{e}(a_{t})\otimes\bm{z}_{t};\;\bm{u}_{1:t}\right),\qquad a_{1:t+1}=a_{1:t}\|a_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">?</mi><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>?</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⊗</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.447em">;</mo><msub><mi>?</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\in\mathcal{V},\qquad\bm{z}_{t+1}=f_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{e}(a_{t})\otimes\bm{z}_{t};\;\bm{u}_{1:t}\right),\qquad a_{1:t+1}=a_{1:t}\|a_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  4045. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  4046. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  4047. </table>
  4048. <p id="S3.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\cdot\otimes\cdot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⊗</mo><mo lspace="0em">⋅</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cdot\otimes\cdot</annotation></semantics></math> is the gate of Eq. (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3.1 Latent feedback decoding ‣ 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) and <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>
  4049. the full stack. The past latents <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{z}_{1:t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>?</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{z}_{1:t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> are not carried explicitly: each is
  4050. already folded into <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\bm{u}_{1:t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>?</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{u}_{1:t}</annotation></semantics></math> and hence into the KV cache, so only <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{z}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>?</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{z}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, which
  4051. the cache never stores, propagates as a recurrence variable.</p>
  4052. </div>
  4053. <section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
  4054. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent feedback improves computational accessibility.</h4>
  4055.  
  4056. <div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4057. <p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> is a deterministic function of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="x_{1:t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{1:t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>, it carries no information the context does not already determine; the gain is computational, not informational. Concretely, re-injection lifts the depth restriction of Eq. (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Bandwidths of a model’s horizonal axis vs. veritical axis. ‣ 2 Background ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), whose reachable set requires <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell^{\prime}<\ell" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo><</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{\prime}<\ell</annotation></semantics></math>, so that every layer, including the lowest, reads the full history,</p>
  4058. <table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
  4059.  
  4060. <tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
  4061. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
  4062. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}}(t,\ell)\;=\;\bigl\{\,(t^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\;:\;t^{\prime}<t,\;0\leq\ell^{\prime}\leq L\,\bigr\},\qquad\bigl\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}}\bigr\rvert=\Theta(TL)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>lf</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo rspace="0.558em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">:</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo><</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mn> 0</mn><mo>≤</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>≤</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mi>lf</mi></msub><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}}(t,\ell)\;=\;\bigl\{\,(t^{\prime},\ell^{\prime})\;:\;t^{\prime}<t,\;0\leq\ell^{\prime}\leq L\,\bigr\},\qquad\bigl\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}}\bigr\rvert=\Theta(TL),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
  4063. <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
  4064. <td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
  4065. </table>
  4066. <p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">shown in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (right). In standard CoT each new token instead accesses only a partially processed view of the context. The improved accessibility is also empirically verified in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Full-bandwidth transformer carries richer information in shallow-layer residuals ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
  4067. </div>
  4068. </section>
  4069. <section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
  4070. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Latent feedback adds draft space.</h4>
  4071.  
  4072. <div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4073. <p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Latent feedback also supplies an implicit scratchpad, relieving the pressure to verbalize intermediate state. State maintenance moves from the sequence axis alone to the depth axis as well: intermediate results can be updated through <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z</annotation></semantics></math> along the stack rather than only by extending the token sequence. This predicts shorter rollouts on reasoning tasks, which Sec. <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Latent feedback enables more concise reasoning ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Full-bandwidth transformer" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> confirms.</p>
  4074. </div>
  4075. </section>
  4076. <section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
  4077. <h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">What latent feedback does not provide.</h4>
  4078.  
  4079. <div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4080. <p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide two important clarifications:</p>
  4081. <ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
  4082. <li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
  4083. <div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
  4084. <p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No mutable register.</span> RNNs and state-space models overwrite a compressed state at each step. Latent feedback is recurrent in form, but past states persist in the KV cache rather than being overwritten, so every earlier state stays directly readable by the current token.</p>
  4085. </div></li>
  4086. <li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
  4087. <div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
  4088. <p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">No added asymptotic depth at decoding time.</span> Latent feedback does not change the serial depth of decoding: with or without it, each step has a depth-<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(L)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">?</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(L)</annotation></semantics></math> graph, so <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> tokens cost <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(TL)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">?</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(TL)</annotation></semantics></math>. What changes is the <em id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bandwidth</em> of the path, with a verbal channel and a continuous channel now evolving in parallel.
  4089. Note that a full-bandwidth transformer can further increase the depth at prefilling time through a multipass prefill, which we will introduce in the following section.</p>
  4090. </div></li>
  4091. </ul>
  4092. </div>
  4093. </section>
  4094. </section>

  4312. <meta property="og:description" content="Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy."/>

  4411.             <span class="descriptor">Abstract:</span>Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.

  4920.     <title>Full-bandwidth transformer</title>
  4921.     <updated>2026-08-09T19:59:45Z</updated>
  4922.     <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08888v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
  4923.     <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
  4924.     <summary>Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.</summary>

  4971. # Full-bandwidth transformer
  4972.  
  4973. ## Authors
  4974. Xi Wang, Ziyang Cai, Zheng Zhan, Harry Dong, Ying Fan, Gustavo de Rosa, Tim Pearce, John Langford
  4975.  
  4976. ## Abstract
  4977. Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the \emph{full-bandwidth transformer}, which widens this channel with \emph{latent feedback}: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly $1.5\times$ more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.
  4978.  
  4979. # Introduction
  4980.  
  4981. Scaling large language models has largely meant increasing model
  4982. parameters and training on more tokens . As pre-training continues to
  4983. scale, however, the availability of high-quality unique data becomes an
  4984. increasingly constraint. This motivates revisiting the scaling axes
  4985. themselves: rather than relying solely on more data, can we extract more
  4986. useful learning signal from each token by allocating more computation to
  4987. it? Recurrent, iterative, and feedback-based computation offer a natural
  4988. way to pursue this direction, but additional FLOPs matter only if they
  4989. translate into richer representations during training or more effective
  4990. computation at inference time.
  4991.  
  4992. Autoregressive transformers expose a particularly underused opportunity
  4993. for such computation. They already contain a feedback loop: the token
  4994. sampled at step $t-1$ becomes the input at step $t$
  4995. (Fig. 1, left). This loop is what lets
  4996. chain-of-thought decoding  perform computation whose depth grows with
  4997. the number of generated tokens . But measured as a communication
  4998. channel, the loop is extremely narrow: Decoding compresses the model’s
  4999. entire top-layer state, a $D$-dimensional vector, down to a single
  5000. symbol carrying at most $\log_2|V|$ bits. Non-verbalized computation is
  5001. not erased—intermediate activations persist in the KV cache and remain
  5002. accessible—but it is *depth-frozen*: a state produced at layer $\ell$ is
  5003. readable only by layers above $\ell$, so it can never return to the
  5004. bottom of the stack for further processing, and the deepest state of
  5005. all, the top layer’s output, is never cached. Verbalization is thus the
  5006. only channel by which information re-enters the bottom layer and
  5007. receives fresh computation, at the cost of being squeezed through a
  5008. single token. The model must either spend tokens narrating its
  5009. intermediate state or recompute that state from scratch at every
  5010. position.
  5011.  
  5012. In this work, we propose *full-bandwidth transformer* where we widen
  5013. this channel to its full width. In particular, we introduce latent
  5014. feedback decoding, which fuses the previous top-layer hidden state with
  5015. the sampled token’s embedding during decoding, through a gated linear
  5016. unit using the state on the value pathway, the token acting as the gate,
  5017. and feeds the result back as the next input
  5018. (Fig. 1 right,
  5019. Sec. 3.1). We call a
  5020. transformer capable of decoding this way a full-bandwidth transformer,
  5021. since its inter-step feedback now carries the entire hidden state rather
  5022. than a thin token. The sampled token is retained, so the model still
  5023. produces ordinary text and can be flexibly trained with standard
  5024. supervised language modeling losses; what changes is that the feedback
  5025. is no longer limited to the token’s identity. By design, this affords
  5026. two things standard decoding lacks: (i) non-verbalized
  5027. state—uncertainty, partial results, plans—can re-enter the bottom of the
  5028. stack with a renewed depth budget and be processed further across steps,
  5029. rather than staying frozen in the cache at the level where it was
  5030. produced; (ii) every layer, including the shallowest, sees the past as
  5031. processed by the *full* stack, not only by the layers beneath it;
  5032. Crucially, these come with almost no architecture changes and extra
  5033. serving cost: the fusion adds two matrix multiplications per generated
  5034. token, attention and the KV cache are untouched, and prefill is run
  5035. either once or, optionally, twice for better performance.
  5036.  
  5037. The obstacle is training. A pretrained model has never seen hidden
  5038. states in its input, so latent feedback cannot simply be switched on at
  5039. inference; and the recurrence it defines is sequential over positions,
  5040. so training on it directly would forfeit the parallel teacher forcing
  5041. that makes transformers efficient to train. We resolve this with a
  5042. *multi-pass* regime
  5043. (Sec. 3.3): each pass shifts the
  5044. previous pass’s hidden states one position rightward, fuses them with
  5045. the token embeddings, and re-runs the stack in parallel across all
  5046. positions, so sequentiality is paid across a handful of passes rather
  5047. than across the sequence. Two ingredients make this practical. A
  5048. *progressive schedule* spends the bulk of training on the ordinary
  5049. single-pass objective such that the run can start from a standard
  5050. pretraining checkpoint and introduces extra feedback passes only late;
  5051. and a *prefix mixin* randomizes where fused inputs begin within a
  5052. sequence, matching the prompt-then-generate structure of inference.
  5053. Empirically, we find the schedule’s composition matters in an unexpected
  5054. way: training with two feedback passes alone produces a recurrence that
  5055. *diverges* once rolled past its trained depth, whereas mixing in as
  5056. little as 3% three-pass batches turns the learned map into a
  5057. *contraction* toward a fixed point that stays stable beyond the trained
  5058. depth
  5059. (Fig. 3).
  5060.  
  5061. Empirically, full-bandwidth transformers convert negligible extra
  5062. inference compute into gains equivalent to substantially more training
  5063. data. Utilizing multiple forward pass for prefill, the
  5064. recurrence-trained model matches no-recurrence baselines trained on
  5065. twice the tokens in both validation loss and multiple-choice accuracy
  5066. (Fig. 4). On free-form generation
  5067. (Fig. 5)—GSM8K, Math500,
  5068. HumanEval, MBPP—latent feedback improves over standard decoding of the
  5069. *same* weights on every task, matches the $2\times$-token baselines, and
  5070. on some tasks approaches baselines trained with up to $5\times$ the
  5071. tokens; the gains carry over through long-context extension and
  5072. instruction tuning
  5073. (Table 1). On base models, latent feedback
  5074. often yields markedly shorter reasoning traces at equal or better
  5075. accuracy
  5076. (Fig. 6 and
  5077. 8)—the behavior the widened
  5078. channel predicts, with computation riding the hidden state instead of
  5079. being verbalized token by token.
  5080.
