  5095.  
  5096.  
  5097. # Background
  5098.  
  5099. Given a vocabulary of size $|V|$ and a $D$-dimensional residual stream,
  5100. a decoder-only LLM maps an input sequence of $T$ tokens, with embeddings
  5101. $\{\bm{e}_t\}_{t=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}$, through $L$
  5102. attention–MLP blocks. The final-layer hidden states
  5103. $\{\bm{h}_t^{L}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ are projected by the language-model head
  5104. $W_{\text{head}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times D}$ to next-token
  5105. distributions:
  5106. $$\bm{h}_t^{L} = f_\theta(\bm{e}_t;\, C), \qquad \bm{e}_t \leftarrow \mathrm{Decode}\!\left(\bm{h}_{t-1}^{L}\right), \quad C= \bm{e}_0, \bm{e}_1, \ldots, \bm{e}_{t-1}.
  5107. \label{eq:standard-decode}$$
  5108.  
  5109. #### KV cache.
  5110.  
  5111. During autoregressive decoding with transformers, previously computed
  5112. keys and values are cached and reused, avoiding repeated computation
  5113. over the prefix. Unlike RNNs and state-space models, which compress
  5114. history into a fixed-size recurrent state, dense-attention transformers
  5115. retain explicit representations of all past tokens, so each new hidden
  5116. state can attend directly to the full cached history.
  5117.  
  5118. #### Bandwidths of a model’s horizonal axis vs. veritical axis.
  5119.  
  5120. It is useful to separate the horizontal axis (across positions) from the
  5121. vertical axis (across depth), because the two carry information at
  5122. different rates. *Horizontally*, dense attention is effectively
  5123. full-bandwidth: when generating token $t$, the layer-$\ell$ state
  5124. $\bm{h}_t^{\ell}$ can read the cached representations of every earlier
  5125. position. *Vertically*, access is restricted: $\bm{h}_t^{\ell}$ cannot
  5126. read any deeper past state $\bm{h}_{t'}^{\ell'}$ with $t'<t$ and
  5127. $\ell'\ge\ell$ (Fig. 1, left). Formally, the states
  5128. reachable when computing position $t$ at layer $\ell$ are
  5129. $$\mathcal{R}_{\text{std}}(t,\ell) = \big\{(t',\ell') : t'<t,\; \ell'<\ell\big\},
  5130. \qquad
  5131. \bigl\lvert \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{std}} \bigr\rvert = \Theta(T\ell),
  5132. \label{eq:std-reach}$$
  5133.  so a shallow layer of a new token sees only a
  5134. *partially processed* view of the past, even though the deeper, more
  5135. fully processed states of those same positions have already been
  5136. computed and sit in the cache. Past computation therefore persists but
  5137. is *depth-frozen* in that the representations produced at layer $\ell$
  5138. is readable only to layers above $\ell$ and can never be routed back
  5139. down for further processing. This is the narrow vertical channel that
  5140. sec. 3.1 widens.
  5141.  
  5142. Importantly, this depth-wise dependency constraint is also what lets
  5143. transformers train in parallel across positions: sequential computation
  5144. is required only across layers, not across tokens. At decoding time,
  5145. however, generation is already sequential over tokens, so the constraint
  5146. buys nothing—opening the door to richer dependencies on past hidden
  5147. states, which we develop next.
  5148.  
  5149. # Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding
  5150.  
  5151. ## Latent feedback decoding
  5152.  
  5153. The central innovation in full-bandwidth transformer is latent feedback
  5154. decoding, which feeds the previous top-layer hidden state back into the
  5155. input. At step $t$,
  5156. $$\bm{h}_{t}^L = f_\theta\!\left(\bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^L;\; C\right), \qquad
  5157.     \textrm{where}~\bm{e}_t \leftarrow \mathrm{Decode}\!\left(\bm{W}^{\textrm{head}}\bm{h}_{t-1}^L\right),\; C=\bm{e}_0, \bm{e}_1 \otimes \bm{h}_0^L,\ldots, \bm{e}_{t-1} \otimes \bm{h}_{t-2}^L
  5158.     \label{eq:latent-feedback}$$
  5159.  where $f_\theta$ is the $L$-layer
  5160. transformer stack, $\cdot \otimes \cdot$ fuses the sampled token’s
  5161. embedding with the previous latent state, and $C$ is the past context
  5162. (the KV cache of all earlier positions). Standard decoding
  5163. (Eq. [eq:standard-decode]) is the
  5164. special case in which only the sampled token crosses between steps.
  5165.  
  5166. The fusion $\otimes$ is a gated linear unit:
  5167. $$\label{eq:glu_cross}
  5168. \bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1} = \bm{W}^U\bm{h}_{t-1} \odot \sigma(\bm{W}^G\bm{e}_{t}),$$
  5169. with $\bm{W}^U, \bm{W}^G\in \mathbb{R}^{D\times D}$. The asymmetry is
  5170. deliberate: the hidden state occupies the value pathway, while the token
  5171. embedding enters only as a multiplicative gate. A symmetric fusion such
  5172. as $\bm{e}_t + \bm{W}\bm{h}_{t-1}$ would leave a shortcut open: the
  5173. model could suppress the state pathway, recover the plain token input,
  5174. and reach ordinary pretraining loss, leaving the wide channel unused.
  5175. That shortcut is especially tempting when training starts from a
  5176. standard checkpoint whose low loss the additive path can reproduce.
  5177. Eq. [eq:glu_cross] closes it, since
  5178. discarding $\bm{h}_{t-1}$ discards the input itself, and the token’s
  5179. identity survives only in the $D$-dimensional gating pattern it imposes
  5180. on the state. Reading the state is thereby mandatory rather than
  5181. optional.
  5182.  
  5183. #### Latent feedback is free to serve.
  5184.  
  5185. The added inference cost is independent of context-length and
  5186. model-depth and under $1\%$ per token. The state $\bm{h}_{t-1}^L$ is
  5187. already computed during standard decoding, so the only extra work is the
  5188. fusion: two $D\times D$ matrix multiplications, negligible against a
  5189. forward pass through $L$ blocks. Because fusion preserves the input
  5190. dimension $D$, the architecture, KV-cache layout, and serving stack are
  5191. untouched, and the decoding loop changes by two lines
  5192. (Fig. 2, right). The scheme is also
  5193. vLLM-compatible: we store top-layer states in a dedicated buffer,
  5194. adapting the mechanism used by multi-token-prediction implementations
  5195. (Appendix 10).
  5196.  
  5197. ## Latent feedback decoding vs. standard CoT
  5198.  
  5199. Standard CoT performs serial computation through a single feedback
  5200. channel: each token is appended to the context and becomes the next
  5201. input. The state is the token sequence,
  5202. $$\label{eq:std-transition}
  5203. s_{t+1} = s_t \Vert a_t,
  5204. \qquad
  5205. a_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s_t) \in \mathcal{V},
  5206. \qquad
  5207. s_t = x_{1:t},$$
  5208.  so the only thing crossing between steps is the
  5209. discrete action sequence. The underlying problem-solving state may in
  5210. principle be a deterministic function of the past actions, but
  5211. recovering it from the token history is itself a state-tracking problem,
  5212. and a fixed-depth transformer has only bounded serial computation per
  5213. forward pass. CoT sidesteps this by externalizing intermediate state
  5214. into language: the model writes out partial results, subgoals, and
  5215. bookkeeping, then conditions future computation on the written trace.
  5216.  
  5217. Let $\bm{u}_i = \bm{e}(a_{i-1}) \otimes \bm{z}_{i-1}$ be the fused input
  5218. at position $i$ (with $\bm{u}_1 = \bm{e}_0$), so the attended context is
  5219. $C_t = \bm{u}_{1:t-1}$. The state is $s_t = (a_{1:t},\, \bm{z}_t)$: the
  5220. token trace and the most recent latent. One step for latent feedback
  5221. decoding is
  5222. $$\label{eq:lf-transition}
  5223. a_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s_t) \in \mathcal{V},
  5224. \qquad
  5225. \bm{z}_{t+1} = f_\theta\!\left(\bm{e}(a_t) \otimes \bm{z}_t;\; \bm{u}_{1:t}\right),
  5226. \qquad
  5227. a_{1:t+1} = a_{1:t}\Vert a_t,$$
  5228.  where $\cdot \otimes \cdot$ is the gate
  5229. of Eq. [eq:glu_cross] and $f_\theta$ the full
  5230. stack. The past latents $\bm{z}_{1:t-1}$ are not carried explicitly:
  5231. each is already folded into $\bm{u}_{1:t}$ and hence into the KV cache,
  5232. so only $\bm{z}_t$, which the cache never stores, propagates as a
  5233. recurrence variable.
  5234.  
  5235. #### Latent feedback improves computational accessibility.
  5236.  
  5237. Since $z_{t+1}$ is a deterministic function of $x_{1:t+1}$, it carries
  5238. no information the context does not already determine; the gain is
  5239. computational, not informational. Concretely, re-injection lifts the
  5240. depth restriction of
  5241. Eq. [eq:std-reach], whose reachable set
  5242. requires $\ell'<\ell$, so that every layer, including the lowest, reads
  5243. the full history,
  5244. $$\label{eq:reach-lf}
  5245. \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}}(t,\ell)
  5246. \;=\; \bigl\{\, (t',\ell') \;:\; t' < t,\; 0 \le \ell' \le L \,\bigr\},
  5247. \qquad
  5248. \bigl\lvert \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{lf}} \bigr\rvert = \Theta(TL),$$
  5249.  shown
  5250. in Fig. 1 (right). In standard CoT each new
  5251. token instead accesses only a partially processed view of the context.
  5252. The improved accessibility is also empirically verified in
  5253. Sec. 4.4.
  5254.  
  5255. #### Latent feedback adds draft space.
  5256.  
  5257. Latent feedback also supplies an implicit scratchpad, relieving the
  5258. pressure to verbalize intermediate state. State maintenance moves from
  5259. the sequence axis alone to the depth axis as well: intermediate results
  5260. can be updated through $z$ along the stack rather than only by extending
  5261. the token sequence. This predicts shorter rollouts on reasoning tasks,
  5262. which Sec. 4.3 confirms.
  5263.  
  5264. #### What latent feedback does not provide.
  5265.  
  5266. We provide two important clarifications:
  5267.  
  5268. - **No mutable register.** RNNs and state-space models overwrite a
  5269.   compressed state at each step. Latent feedback is recurrent in form,
  5270.   but past states persist in the KV cache rather than being overwritten,
  5271.   so every earlier state stays directly readable by the current token.
  5272.  
  5273. - **No added asymptotic depth at decoding time.** Latent feedback does
  5274.   not change the serial depth of decoding: with or without it, each step
  5275.   has a depth-$\mathcal{O}(L)$ graph, so $T$ tokens cost
  5276.   $\mathcal{O}(TL)$. What changes is the *bandwidth* of the path, with a
  5277.   verbal channel and a continuous channel now evolving in parallel. Note
  5278.   that a full-bandwidth transformer can further increase the depth at
  5279.   prefilling time through a multipass prefill, which we will introduce
  5280.   in the following section.
  5281.  
  5282. ## Parallel training for latent feedback decoding
  5283.  
  5284.  
  5285.  
  5286. > **Figure 2:** Latent feedback in pseudo-code. Training (left) pays
  5287. sequentiality across k passes,
  5288. each parallel over positions. Inference (right) differs from standard
  5289. decoding by a single line (line 6 vs. the commented line 7): the input
  5290. is the fused state rather than the token embedding alone, reusing the
  5291. state previously used for decoding.
  5292.  
  5293.  
  5294.  
  5295.  
  5296.  
  5297. > **Figure 3:** A small fraction of three-pass batches stabilizes
  5298. long-horizon latent feedback. We test whether the learned
  5299. feedback map extrapolates beyond the number of passes seen during
  5300. training by repeatedly applying fused prefill passes. A model trained
  5301. with only single- and two-pass batches fails beyond its trained horizon:
  5302. validation loss increases and the hidden-state update size oscillates.
  5303. Adding a small fraction of three-pass batches makes the iterates stable:
  5304. (left) validation loss remains flat across many
  5305. feedback steps, and (right) the hidden-state change
  5306. ∥h(k) − h(k−1)∥
  5307. decays toward a small plateau. This diagnostic uses repeated feedback
  5308. passes as a proxy for the long-horizon self-composition encountered
  5309. during latent-feedback decoding.
  5310.  
  5311.  
  5312.  
  5313. At decoding time, latent feedback unrolls over generated positions. Let
  5314. $\bm{u}_t$ be the input actually fed to the transformer stack at
  5315. position $t$. The first position receives a plain token embedding, while
  5316. each later position receives a fusion of the current token embedding and
  5317. the previous top-layer state:
  5318. $$\begin{aligned}
  5319.     \bm{u}_1 &= \bm{e}_1,
  5320.     &\bm{h}_1 &= f_\theta(\bm{u}_1; C_1), \\
  5321.     \bm{u}_t &= \bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1},
  5322.     &\bm{h}_t &= f_\theta(\bm{u}_t; C_t), \qquad t \ge 2 .
  5323. \end{aligned}
  5324. \label{eq:decode-unroll}$$
  5325.  Here $\cdot \otimes \cdot$ is the gated
  5326. fusion of Eq. [eq:glu_cross], and $C_t$ is the KV
  5327. cache over the previous inputs $\bm{u}_{1:t-1}$. Thus the stack sees the
  5328. input sequence
  5329. $$\bm{e}_1,\
  5330.     \bm{e}_2 \otimes \bm{h}_1,\
  5331.     \bm{e}_3 \otimes \bm{h}_2,\
  5332.     \bm{e}_4 \otimes \bm{h}_3,\ldots$$
  5333.  rather than plain embeddings
  5334. alone. Since a standard next-token-prediction model is trained only on
  5335. plain token embeddings in this slot, full-bandwidth transformers must be
  5336. trained on these latent-feedback inputs as well.
  5337.  
  5338. The exact recurrence of
  5339. Eq. [eq:decode-unroll] is sequential
  5340. in $t$: the input at position $t$ depends on the completed forward pass
  5341. at position $t-1$, so training on it directly would sacrifice the
  5342. parallel teacher forcing that makes transformers efficient to pre-train.
  5343. We instead adopt a multi-forward-pass approximation. For each position
  5344. in the sequence, we compute the top-layer state several times, writing
  5345. $\bm{h}_t^{(k)}$ for the state at position $t$ on pass $k$ (the layer
  5346. superscript $L$ is omitted throughout this section):
  5347. $$\begin{aligned}
  5348. \bm{h}_t^{(1)} &= f_\theta(\bm{e}_t;\, C^{(1)}),
  5349.   & C^{(1)} &= \bm{e}_1, \ldots, \bm{e}_{t-1}, \label{eq:pass1}\\
  5350. \bm{h}_t^{(2)} &= f_\theta\!\big(\bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^{(1)};\, C^{(2)}\big),
  5351.   & C^{(2)} &= \bm{e}_1,\, \bm{e}_2 \otimes \bm{h}_1^{(1)},\, \ldots,\, \bm{e}_{t-1} \otimes \bm{h}_{t-2}^{(1)}, \label{eq:pass2}\\
  5352.   &\qquad\ldots \nonumber \\
  5353. \bm{h}_t^{(k)} &= f_\theta\!\big(\bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^{(k-1)};\, C^{(k)}\big),
  5354.   & C^{(k)} &= \bm{e}_1,\, \bm{e}_2 \otimes \bm{h}_1^{(k-1)},\, \ldots,\, \bm{e}_{t-1} \otimes \bm{h}_{t-2}^{(k-1)}. \label{eq:pass3}
  5355. \end{aligned}$$
  5356.  The first pass is the ordinary no-feedback forward pass
  5357. ($\bm{h}_t^{(1)} \equiv \bm{h}_t$); each subsequent pass shifts the
  5358. previous pass’s states one position rightward, fuses them with the token
  5359. embeddings, and re-runs the full stack in parallel across all positions,
  5360. since every state it requires was completed in the previous pass.
  5361.  
  5362. We then apply the standard teacher-forced next-token-prediction loss[^1]
  5363. to the outputs of every pass. Retaining the first-pass loss preserves
  5364. the model’s no-feedback mode of operation, which is what processes the
  5365. prompt at inference time. We do not detach the gradient, so the loss
  5366. from later passes backpropagates into earlier passes’ latent states,
  5367. acting as an auxiliary objective; this does increase the memory
  5368. footprint. The overall objective is
  5369. $$\mathcal{L}^{K}(\theta)
  5370. = \underbrace{\sum_{t=1}^{T} -\log p_\theta\!\left(x_{t+1} \mid \bm{e}_{1:t}\right)}_{\text{standard NTP objective}}
  5371. \;+\; \lambda \,\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=2}^{K} \sum_{t=1}^{T}
  5372. -\log p_\theta\!\left(x_{t+1} \mid \bm{e}_{1:t}^{(k)}\right),
  5373. \label{eq:recur-loss}$$
  5374.  where
  5375. $\bm{e}_{1:t}^{(k)} = \bm{e}_1,\, \bm{e}_2 \otimes \bm{h}_1^{(k-1)},\, \ldots,\, \bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^{(k-1)}$
  5376. are the pass-$k$ fused inputs of
  5377. Eqs. [eq:pass2]–[eq:pass3]. In all experiments we set
  5378. $\lambda = 1$ without any tuning.
  5379.  
  5380. A pseudo code is shown in
  5381. Fig. 2 left. We refer to this training
  5382. scheme as *temporal parallelism*, following a common strategy for
  5383. parallelizing recurrent computation during training . Each pass is a
  5384. Jacobi-style update of the latent-feedback recurrence: the hidden states
  5385. from the previous pass are shifted one position to the right, fused with
  5386. the token embeddings, and used to update all positions in parallel. Each
  5387. additional pass therefore advances latent feedback by one token. After
  5388. $k$ passes, a top-layer state from position $t$ can affect the input at
  5389. positions up to $t+k-1$, so $k$ passes train the feedback transition
  5390. over a horizon of $k-1$ token steps. Training thus pays sequentiality
  5391. across passes rather than across positions, reducing a length-$T$
  5392. recurrent unroll to $k$ parallel transformer evaluations, at roughly
  5393. $k\times$ the compute of standard teacher forcing. The learned local
  5394. transition is nevertheless the same one used during decoding, where
  5395. latent feedback is applied causally once per generated token.
  5396.  
  5397. #### Feedback-pass scheduling.
  5398.  
  5399. At decoding time the feedback loop unrolls indefinitely, so the trained
  5400. map must remain stable under many more self-compositions than any
  5401. training budget can simulate; yet running many passes throughout
  5402. training is prohibitively expensive, since each pass multiplies the cost
  5403. of the run. Scheduling the number of forward passes—how many, and
  5404. when—is therefore central to making latent-feedback training practical.
  5405.  
  5406. *How many passes.* We choose the number of passes by checking whether
  5407. the iterated feedback map reaches a stable fixed point: a depth beyond
  5408. which additional passes neither change the hidden states substantially
  5409. nor improve the loss. This stability is easier to obtain than in
  5410. architectures that repeatedly recompute the entire input (e.g. a loop
  5411. transformer), because each feedback pass keeps the token embedding fixed
  5412. and updates only the hidden-state pathway through the gate. In practice,
  5413. this means the goal is not to train at the full inference horizon, but
  5414. to train the feedback map until it becomes stable under further
  5415. self-composition.
  5416.  
  5417. *When to introduce feedback passes.* Because feedback passes are
  5418. expensive, most of training uses the standard single-pass objective. We
  5419. introduce latent feedback progressively in the middle of training: first
  5420. with two-pass batches, and later with a small fraction of batches with
  5421. more passes. This lets the run begin from an ordinary pretrained
  5422. checkpoint, spend the bulk of its compute on standard teacher forcing,
  5423. and pay the extra feedback-pass cost only mid-training, when it is
  5424. needed to stabilize the feedback map.
  5425.  
  5426. Fig. 3 illustrates the
  5427. feasibility of the scheduling. We studied a 1B model trained on 200B
  5428. tokens. A model trained with only single- and two-pass batches (75%
  5429. single-pass, 25% two-pass; green) performs well at the trained depth but
  5430. fails to extrapolate: beyond that depth, validation loss rises sharply
  5431. and the hidden-state change $\|\bm{h}^{(k)} - \bm{h}^{(k-1)}\|$
  5432. oscillates rather than decays, indicating that the iterates have left
  5433. the trained state distribution. Adding only 3% three-pass batches (75%
  5434. single-pass, 22% two-pass, 3% three-pass; blue) qualitatively changes
  5435. the behavior: validation loss remains flat through $30$ feedback steps,
  5436. and the hidden-state change decays to a small plateau. This suggests
  5437. that the learned feedback map behaves like a contraction toward a fixed
  5438. point, making feedback depths far beyond those seen in training stable
  5439. in our tests. The same extrapolation behavior carries over to inference:
  5440. hundred-token rollouts show no sign of breakdown
  5441. (Fig. 5, solid green line), and
  5442. we observe similar stability under $k=1000$ feedback passes
  5443. (Fig. 10 in the appendix).
  5444.  
  5445. #### Prefix mixin.
  5446.  
  5447. A distribution mismatch remains between multi-pass training and
  5448. inference. At decoding time a sequence is heterogeneous: prompt
  5449. positions carry plain token embeddings (processed by a single prefill
  5450. pass), while generated positions carry fused inputs. In the passes of
  5451. Eqs. [eq:pass2]–[eq:pass3], by contrast, *every* position
  5452. beyond the first is fused. A model trained only on fully-fused passes
  5453. therefore encounters an out-of-distribution boundary at inference,
  5454. precisely where the prompt ends and generation begins. To close this gap
  5455. we apply a *prefix mixin*: in each pass beyond the first, we sample a
  5456. random prefix length $p$ and revert positions $t \leq p$ to plain
  5457. embeddings, fusing only the suffix. Training thus covers sequences that
  5458. switch from plain to fused inputs at an arbitrary point, i.e. the
  5459. structure of single-prefill inference. Alternatively, the prompt itself
  5460. can be run through a second, fused prefill pass so that all positions
  5461. match the fused distribution; the mixin removes the need for this, but
  5462. we support both, corresponding to the “identical or doubled prefill”
  5463. overhead stated in the abstract.
  5464.  
  5465. #### Stability recipes for long feedback horizons.
  5466.  
  5467. At inference time, latent feedback may be applied for hundreds or
  5468. thousands of generated tokens, far beyond the few feedback passes used
  5469. during training. We therefore use several lightweight stabilization
  5470. techniques to keep the feedback map well behaved under long
  5471. self-composition.
  5472.  
  5473. - **Stationary hidden-state scale.** We keep the magnitude of carried
  5474.   state $\bm{h}_t^L$ bounded as feedback is repeatedly applied. To
  5475.   prevent the top-layer state norm from growing with depth, we use depth
  5476.   scaling  so that
  5477.   $\left\lVert\bm{h}_t^L\right\rVert \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ rather than
  5478.   $\mathcal{O}(L)$, as can occur in a standard pre-norm model. We also
  5479.   apply RMSNorm to the fused input $\bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^L$
  5480.   before feeding it into the model.
  5481.  
  5482. - **Shared input basis with weight tying.** The model processes two
  5483.   types of inputs: plain token embeddings during standard prefill, and
  5484.   fused hidden-state/token inputs during latent-feedback decoding. We
  5485.   therefore encourage the embedding space and top-layer hidden-state
  5486.   space to remain in a compatible basis by tying the weights of the
  5487.   embedding layer and readout layer, reducing the burden on the fusion
  5488.   weights to learn a large corrective rotation between the two input
  5489.   distributions.
  5490.  
  5491. - **Noise regularization.** During training, we add small jitter noise
  5492.   to the carried hidden state before fusion,
  5493. $$\label{eq:jitter_noise}
  5494.           \bm{h}_t^L
  5495.           =
  5496.           f_\theta\!\left(
  5497.               \bm{e}_t \otimes \bm{h}_{t-1}^L + \epsilon;
  5498.               C
  5499.           \right),
  5500.           \qquad
  5501.           \epsilon \sim \mathrm{Uniform}[-\sigma,\sigma]^D .$$
  5502.  This
  5503.   exposes the feedback map to a local neighborhood around each training
  5504.   state, making it less sensitive to small deviations that can
  5505.   accumulate over long feedback horizons.

  5511. ## Latent-feedback training improves pre-training data efficiency
  5512.  
  5513. Beyond enabling latent feedback at decoding time, the feedback passes
  5514. also act as an auxiliary training signal on the hidden states. In the
  5515. standard next-token-prediction loss, the top-layer state $\bm{h}_t^L$ is
  5516. supervised only through the prediction of the next token. In later
  5517. feedback passes, however, $\bm{h}_t^L$ is shifted, fused into the input
  5518. of subsequent positions, and can influence losses at multiple future
  5519. positions through causal attention. Thus gradients from later
  5520. predictions backpropagate into earlier hidden states, encouraging them
  5521. to be reusable as inputs rather than merely predictive at the output
  5522. layer.
  5523.  
  5524. Empirically, this improves pre-training data efficiency even when latent
  5525. feedback is not used at decoding time. When evaluated with standard
  5526. decoding, models trained with the latent-feedback objective improve on
  5527. LM Eval and free-form generation tasks relative to comparable models
  5528. trained only with the ordinary next-token objective. We can therefore
  5529. view latent-feedback training as a way to spend additional training-time
  5530. compute on the same token stream, improving the representations without
  5531. changing the serving-time decoding pipeline.
  5532.  
  5533. Latent-feedback training also enables a simple form of prefill-time
  5534. test-time scaling. At evaluation, we can apply $k$ additional fused
  5535. passes over the prompt using
  5536. Eqs. [eq:pass2]–[eq:pass3]. These passes refine the prompt
  5537. states before generation begins, improving perplexity and downstream
  5538. accuracy at the cost of $k$ extra parallel prefill forward passes. See
  5539. Sec. 4.1.

Authors and Institution(s) The research paper "Full-bandwidth transformer" was authored by: * **Xi Wang** (Johns Hopkins University, and Microsoft AI Frontiers) * **Ziyang Cai** (Princeton University, and Microsoft AI Frontiers) * **Zheng Zhan** (Microsoft) * **Harry Dong** (Microsoft) * **Ying Fan** (Microsoft) * **Gustavo de Rosa** (Microsoft) * **Tim Pearce** (Microsoft) * **John Langford** (Microsoft) Correspondence is attributed to Xi Wang at Johns Hopkins University and John Langford at Microsoft. ### 2. How This Work Fits into the Broader Research Landscape The development of large language models (LLMs) has largely been characterized by increases in model parameters and the volume of training data. However, the availability of high-quality, unique training data is becoming a limiting factor as models continue to scale. This constraint motivates research into alternative scaling axes, specifically exploring how to extract more useful learning signals from each token by allocating additional computation. Autoregressive transformers, while effective, possess a design characteristic that presents an opportunity for such computational refinement. They employ a feedback loop where a sampled token from the previous step becomes the input for the current step. This mechanism enables sequential reasoning, as seen in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decoding, where computation depth can grow with the number of generated tokens. However, the feedback channel in standard transformers is narrow; it compresses the model's top-layer hidden state into a single symbol (the token). Non-verbalized computation, while present in the KV cache, remains "depth-frozen," meaning states produced at higher layers cannot be explicitly re-processed by lower layers in subsequent steps. This limits the ability of the model to carry forward rich, non-verbalized intermediate states for further processing, often necessitating the explicit verbalization of reasoning steps. This research addresses this limitation by proposing a method to widen this vertical feedback channel. It aligns with other efforts to enhance transformer efficiency and capabilities, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state-space models, which explicitly maintain a recurrent state. However, it distinguishes itself by integrating this broader feedback mechanism directly into the transformer architecture with minimal modifications, aiming to leverage the existing strengths of transformers, such as parallel training and dense attention, while mitigating the described depth-wise information flow constraint. It also relates to emerging work on recurrent and iterative computation in transformers, like Feedback Transformers, T²MLR, Latent Recurrent Transformers, and Loop Transformers, by aiming to improve data efficiency and inference performance through richer internal state management. ### 3. Key Objectives and Motivation The primary motivation for this research stems from the observation that while autoregressive transformers have a feedback loop, this channel is significantly constrained. The entire top-layer hidden state, a high-dimensional vector, is effectively compressed into a single sampled token before re-entering the model's input stack. This "narrow vertical feedback channel" means that non-verbalized computation—such as partial results, uncertainties, or complex plans—cannot directly re-enter the bottom of the transformer stack for renewed processing. Instead, this intermediate state is either discarded at the top layer or remains "depth-frozen" in the KV cache, accessible only to layers above its point of origin. Consequently, the model must either explicitly verbalize its intermediate reasoning steps, consuming valuable tokens, or recompute this state from scratch at each new position. This represents an underutilized computational opportunity. Against this background, the key objectives of this work are: 1. **To widen the inter-step feedback channel:** Introduce a mechanism, termed "latent feedback decoding," that fuses the previous top-layer hidden state with the sampled token embedding. This allows the full, high-bandwidth hidden state to re-enter the model as input for the next decoding step, thereby providing a "full-bandwidth transformer." 2. **To enable renewed processing of non-verbalized computation:** By feeding back the full hidden state, the model can allow non-verbalized information to re-enter the bottom of the stack with a fresh computational budget, enabling further processing across decoding steps without being limited to token verbalization. This also ensures that even shallow layers can access a more fully processed view of the past, leveraging computation from the entire stack. 3. **To maintain architectural compatibility and low inference overhead:** Implement this enhanced feedback mechanism with minimal modifications to the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. The goal is to achieve significant benefits with negligible per-token decoding overhead during inference. 4. **To develop a training methodology that supports parallel training:** Address the challenge of training a recurrent feedback mechanism without sacrificing the efficiency of parallel teacher forcing. This involves designing a multi-pass objective and scheduling strategy that can introduce latent feedback progressively during pre-training and ensure stability for long-horizon rollouts. 5. **To empirically demonstrate performance improvements:** Evaluate whether the proposed full-bandwidth transformer improves validation loss, 5-shot language model evaluation, and free-form generation on tasks such as math and coding, as well as instruction-tuned performance. A specific aim is to assess if the approach can match or exceed the performance of standard transformers trained with substantially more tokens, and potentially lead to more concise reasoning traces. In essence, the motivation is to make transformers more computationally efficient and capable by enabling a richer, continuous flow of internal state information across decoding steps, moving beyond the bottleneck of discrete token feedback. ### 4. Methodology and Approach The core of this work is the introduction of **latent feedback decoding** within a "full-bandwidth transformer" framework, accompanied by a specialized parallel training regime. #### 4.1 Latent Feedback Decoding The primary innovation involves modifying the input to the transformer at each decoding step. In a standard autoregressive transformer, the sampled token from step `t-1` becomes the input for step `t`. In latent feedback decoding, the input at step `t` is a fusion of the current sampled token's embedding ($e_t$) and the previous step's top-layer hidden state ($h^L_{t-1}$). The fusion operation is defined as: $u_t = e_t \otimes h^L_{t-1}$ where $f_\theta$ is the L-layer transformer stack, $u_t$ is the fused input, and $C$ is the past context (KV cache). The fusion operator $\otimes$ is specifically a **gated linear unit (GLU)**: $e_t \otimes h_{t-1} = W_U h_{t-1} \odot \sigma(W_G e_t)$ Here, $W_U$ and $W_G$ are learned DxD matrices. The previous hidden state ($h_{t-1}$) occupies the value pathway, while the token embedding ($e_t$) acts as a multiplicative gate. This asymmetric design is deliberate, as a symmetric fusion (e.g., addition) could allow the model to ignore the hidden state and revert to standard token input, especially when starting from a pre-trained checkpoint. By making reading the hidden state mandatory through the gate, the model is compelled to use this wider channel. This approach offers two key benefits over standard decoding: 1. **Non-verbalized state re-entry:** Intermediate computations, uncertainties, or partial results within the hidden state can re-enter the bottom of the stack, receiving a fresh computational budget across layers, rather than being "depth-frozen." 2. **Full stack accessibility:** Every layer, including the shallowest, can access a view of the past that has been processed by the entire depth of the transformer, rather than only by layers beneath it. Crucially, this modification incurs negligible inference cost, adding only two DxD matrix multiplications per generated token. The core transformer architecture, KV cache layout, and serving stack remain unchanged. The scheme is also compatible with existing inference systems like vLLM by storing top-layer states in a dedicated buffer. #### 4.2 Latent Feedback Decoding vs. Standard Chain-of-Thought (CoT) The paper differentiates latent feedback from standard CoT. While both perform serial computation, CoT externalizes intermediate state into language, using tokens as the sole feedback channel. This requires the model to verbalize its internal progress. Latent feedback, in contrast, introduces an implicit scratchpad, allowing state maintenance to occur along the depth axis through the hidden state $z$, reducing the pressure to verbalize. This is hypothesized to lead to more concise reasoning traces. The improvement is computational, not informational, as the hidden state $z_{t+1}$ is a deterministic function of the context. The "reachability" set for computation is significantly expanded, allowing any layer at position $t$ to access the fully processed states of all previous positions. #### 4.3 Parallel Training for Latent Feedback Decoding A significant challenge is training this recurrent mechanism without sacrificing the parallel teacher forcing efficiency of transformers. Direct unrolling of Eq. (8) would be sequential. The solution is a **multi-forward-pass approximation**, termed "temporal parallelism": 1. **First pass:** Standard no-feedback forward pass, $h^{(1)}_t = f_\theta(e_t; C^{(1)})$. 2. **Subsequent passes (k > 1):** For each pass $k$, the previous pass's top-layer states ($h^{(k-1)}_{t-1}$) are shifted one position right, fused with the current token embeddings ($e_t \otimes h^{(k-1)}_{t-1}$), and the full transformer stack is re-run in parallel across all positions. $h^{(k)}_t = f_\theta(e_t \otimes h^{(k-1)}_{t-1}; C^{(k)})$. Each additional pass effectively advances latent feedback by one token step. The standard next-token-prediction loss is applied to the outputs of *every* pass, with gradients backpropagating through earlier passes' latent states. This provides an auxiliary training signal, encouraging hidden states to be reusable as inputs rather than solely predictive at the output layer. **Feedback-pass scheduling:** To manage computational cost and ensure stability for long inference rollouts, a progressive schedule is employed. Most of pre-training uses the standard single-pass objective. Latent feedback is introduced later, initially with two-pass batches, and then a small fraction (e.g., 3%) of three-pass batches. This small fraction of deeper passes was empirically found to stabilize the learned feedback map, making it behave like a contraction towards a fixed point, enabling stable extrapolation far beyond the training horizon (e.g., 1000 feedback steps in tests). **Prefix mixin:** To mitigate distribution mismatch between training (where all non-prompt positions are fused) and inference (where a prompt is followed by fused generation), a random prefix length $p$ is sampled. For positions $t \le p$, plain embeddings are used, and fusion only applies to the suffix. **Stability recipes for long feedback horizons:** Several techniques ensure the feedback map remains well-behaved under many self-compositions at inference time: * **Stationary hidden-state scale:** Depth scaling and RMSNorm on the fused input prevent state norms from growing indefinitely. * **Shared input basis with weight tying:** Tying embedding and readout layer weights encourages compatibility between token embedding space and top-layer hidden state space. * **Noise regularization:** Adding jitter noise to the carried hidden state during training exposes the feedback map to a local neighborhood, improving robustness. #### 4.4 Training Details Models were 1B-parameter decoder-only causal language models (details in Appendix A), with 24 layers, 1536-dimensional hidden states, and specific attention configurations (gated grouped-query attention, QK RMS normalization, rotary positions, sliding window with occasional full attention). Training utilized the NorMuon optimizer for matrix parameters and Adam for others, with a WSD learning-rate schedule, warmup steps, cooldown, and z-loss. Models were trained on the Phi-4 data mixture with a context length of 8192, up to 400B tokens. Compute is reported as "token-equivalent compute" (training tokens × average forward passes per batch). Jitter noise with $\sigma=0.02$ was applied. ### 5. Main Findings and Results The research presents several key findings across different evaluation paradigms, demonstrating the effectiveness of full-bandwidth transformers. #### 5.1 Fused Prefilling Improves Non-Generative Performance The study evaluated performance on validation loss and 5-shot LM Eval accuracy (across 10 tasks) by applying additional fused prefill passes over the prompt (re-running the transformer stack on fused inputs) before generation. * **Front-loaded gains:** The majority of the improvement in both validation perplexity and LM Eval accuracy occurred after the *first* fused prefill pass, indicating the significant benefit of initially exposing top-layer hidden states to the input layer. Subsequent passes offered diminishing returns. * **Low cost when unused:** Even when evaluated as an ordinary transformer with zero feedback passes, the latent-feedback trained model showed only a small increase in validation loss compared to a standard baseline, while already improving average LM Eval accuracy. This suggests the training objective provides value even without explicit latent feedback at inference. * **Data efficiency:** A small amount of prefill-time compute enabled performance comparable to models trained with substantially more data. For instance, a 100B-token full-bandwidth transformer with two feedback passes reached the performance level of a 200B-token standard baseline. Similarly, a 200B-token full-bandwidth transformer matched a 400B-token standard baseline. This implies a data efficiency improvement of approximately 2x for a modest inference-time computational overhead. #### 5.2 Latent Feedback Decoding Improves Decoding Performance The paper assessed open-ended generation performance on tasks including GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval, and MBPP, comparing three decoding regimes: * **STANDARD:** Standard transformer decoding. * **SOFT:** Single-pass prefill, then latent feedback decoding. * **FUSED:** Two-pass prefill (prompt refined with latent feedback), then latent feedback decoding. Key observations: * **Consistent gains:** SOFT decoding consistently improved over STANDARD decoding across all tasks and training scales (100B-400B tokens). These gains were solely from the decoding mechanism, with fixed model weights. * **Task-dependent regime preference:** SOFT decoding yielded the largest improvements on math tasks (e.g., MATH-500 accuracy improved from 0.27 to 0.37 for the 200B model), suggesting benefits for reasoning during generation. FUSED decoding was generally stronger for coding tasks (e.g., HumanEval improved from 0.31 to 0.34 for the 200B model), indicating the utility of a deeper, refined prompt representation before generation. * **Outperforming larger baselines:** Under latent feedback, the 200B recurrent model achieved performance comparable to or exceeding standard baselines trained with 2-5 times more tokens (e.g., nearing the 1T standard baseline on GSM8K and HumanEval). * **Instruction tuning portability:** The performance improvements from both SOFT and FUSED decoding persisted after long-context extension and instruction tuning, outperforming matched standard baselines on all four tasks (e.g., GSM8K from 64.5% to 67.9% for 200B model after tuning). #### 5.3 Latent Feedback Enables More Concise Reasoning On base models, SOFT decoding often produced notably shorter reasoning traces compared to STANDARD decoding while maintaining or improving accuracy. This behavior is exemplified in qualitative outputs on MATH-500, where the full-bandwidth transformer provides more direct answers without extensive verbalization of intermediate steps. This supports the hypothesis that the widened feedback channel allows non-verbalized computation to be carried in the hidden state, reducing the need for explicit token-by-token narration. This effect was observed to diminish after instruction tuning, which the authors attribute to the off-policy nature of tuning data that typically mimics verbose, standard reasoning traces. #### 5.4 Full-bandwidth Transformer Carries Richer Information in Shallow-Layer Residuals To directly verify the increased bandwidth, synthetic state-tracking tasks (Completion tracking, Delayed memory, Multi-register latest-write tracking) were used. Linear probes were trained at various residual-stream depths to predict binary states. * **Shallow layer access:** Under one-step recurrent prefilling, the target state (e.g., whether a counter reached a required value or an initial binary state) became nearly perfectly decodable at Layer 0 (input layer), even across varying input lengths and distractions. In contrast, standard prefilling required multiple layers of computation to reconstruct this global state, with Layer 0 performance near chance. * **Confirmation of mechanism:** This demonstrates that recurrent prefilling provides a high-bandwidth shortcut, transporting globally aggregated information into shallow computation, which aligns with the theoretical prediction of the full-bandwidth view. The "full recurrent" prefilling (where feedback is applied throughout the sequence) performed best on more complex tasks involving multiple registers and overwrites, showing the benefit of maintaining state over long sequences. ### 6. Significance and Potential Impact This research presents the full-bandwidth transformer as a method to enhance the computational capabilities of large language models, offering several areas of significance and potential impact: 1. **Improved Data Efficiency:** The primary impact is the ability to extract more learning signal from each training token. By re-injecting the full top-layer hidden state, the model can achieve performance comparable to or exceeding standard transformers trained with substantially more data (e.g., 1.5x to 5x more tokens) for a given model size. This is particularly significant in an era where the availability of high-quality unique training data is becoming a bottleneck for scaling. It suggests a path towards developing more capable models without exclusively relying on ever-increasing datasets. 2. **Enhanced Inference Capabilities with Minimal Overhead:** The latent feedback decoding mechanism provides a direct performance boost during inference, improving accuracy on both non-generative (LM Eval) and free-form generation (math, coding) tasks. Crucially, this is achieved with negligible per-token decoding overhead (two DxD matrix multiplications), maintaining the high inference speed characteristic of transformers. This makes the approach practical for deployment in real-world applications where latency is critical. 3. **More Concise and Effective Reasoning:** The observation that latent feedback can lead to shorter, yet equally or more accurate, reasoning traces on base models suggests that the widened channel enables more implicit, internal computation. This could reduce the verbosity often seen in LLM outputs, leading to more direct and efficient problem-solving. While this effect was mitigated after instruction tuning on verbose datasets, it opens avenues for developing new "on-policy" fine-tuning strategies that leverage this conciseness. 4. **Architectural Simplicity and Compatibility:** The method integrates with existing transformer architectures with minimal structural changes. It modifies only the input construction and leverages existing KV cache mechanisms, preserving the core transformer design and its advantages, such as parallel training. This ease of integration could facilitate adoption across various transformer-based models and systems. 5. **New Scaling Axis for LLMs:** This work contributes to the evolving understanding of LLM scaling laws. Beyond simply increasing model parameters or training data, it highlights "computation per token" as a valuable scaling axis. By spending additional training-time FLOPs on a given token stream to unlock a richer decoding regime, the research offers an alternative strategy for building more powerful models, especially when data or GPU pod size become limiting factors. 6. **Foundation for Future Research:** The progressive feedback-pass scheduling and stability recipes offer insights for training complex recurrent mechanisms within transformer contexts. This could inform future research on auxiliary training objectives, more principled recurrence scheduling, and the application of similar high-bandwidth feedback loops to even larger-scale models or different modalities. The observed behavior of the learned map as a contraction towards a fixed point also points towards deeper theoretical investigations into the stability of such recurrent systems. === https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2608.08888.md STATUS 200 FINAL https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2608.08888.md TYPE text/markdown; charset=utf-8 LEN 76422 === Full-bandwidth transformer Full-bandwidth transformer Xi Wang 1,†,* , Ziyang Cai 2,† , Zheng Zhan 3 , Harry Dong 3 , Ying Fan 3 , Gustavo de Rosa 3 , Tim Pearce 3 , John Langford 3,* 1 Johns Hopkins University 2 Princeton University 3 Microsoft Abstract Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps remains narrow: only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack, while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. We introduce the full-bandwidth transformer, which widens this channel with latent feedback: at each decoding step, the previous top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back as the next input. Latent feedback lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget, while preserving the standard transformer architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective. To train full-bandwidth transformers without losing parallel teacher forcing, we use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. We train 1B-parameter full-bandwidth transformers up to 400B tokens and find that latent feedback improves validation loss, 5-shot language-model evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, full-bandwidth transformers match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly 1.5× more tokens, and manage to produce shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy. 1 Introduction Scaling large language models has largely meant increasing model parameters and training on more tokens (Kaplan et al., 2020). As pre-training continues to scale, however, the availability of high-quality unique data becomes an increasingly constraint. This motivates revisiting the scaling axes themselves: rather than relying solely on more data, can we extract more useful learning signal from each token by allocating more computation to it? Recurrent, iterative, and feedback-based computation offer a natural way to pursue this direction, but additional FLOPs matter only if they translate into richer representations during training or more effective computation at inference time. Autoregressive transformers expose a particularly underused opportunity for such computation. They already contain a feedback loop: the token sampled at step t − 1 becomes the input at step t (Fig. 1, left). This loop is what lets chain-of-thought decoding (Wei et al., 2022) perform computation whose depth grows with the number of generated tokens (Li et al., 2024b). But measured as a communication channel, the loop is extremely narrow: Decoding compresses the model’s entire top-layer state, a D-dimensional vector, down to a single symbol carrying at most log 2 |V | bits. Non-verbalized computation is not erased—intermediate activations persist in the KV cache and remain accessible—but it is depth-frozen: a state produced at layer ℓ is readable only by layers above ℓ, so it can never return to the bottom of the stack for further processing, and the deepest state of all, the top layer’s output, is never cached. Verbalization is thus the only channel by which information re-enters the bottom layer and receives fresh computation, at the cost of being squeezed through a single token. The model must either spend tokens narrating its intermediate state or recompute that state from scratch at every position. In this work, we propose full-bandwidth transformer where we widen this channel to its full width. In particular, we introduce latent feedback decoding, which fuses the previous top-layer hidden state with the sampled token’s embedding during decoding, through a gated linear unit using the state on the value pathway, the token acting as the gate, and feeds the result back as the next input (Fig. 1 right, Sec. 3.1). We call a transformer capable of decoding this way a full-bandwidth transformer, since its inter-step feedback now carries the entire hidden state rather than a * Correspondence to Xi Wang <xwang457@cs.jhu.edu>, John Langford <jcl@microsoft.com>. † Work done during an internship at Microsoft AI Frontiers. 1 arXiv:2608.08888v1 [cs.AI] 9 Aug 2026 Full-bandwidth transformer Figure 1: Standard decoding vs. latent feedback decoding. The sampled token is retained, so the model still produces ordinary text and can be flexibly trained with standard supervised language modeling losses; what changes is that the feedback is no longer limited to the token’s identity. By design, this affords two things standard decoding lacks: (i) non-verbalized state—uncertainty, partial results, plans—can re-enter the bottom of the stack with a renewed depth budget and be processed further across steps, rather than staying frozen in the cache at the level where it was produced; (ii) every layer, including the shallowest, sees the past as processed by the full stack, not only by the layers beneath it; Crucially, these come with almost no architecture changes and extra serving cost: the fusion adds two matrix multiplications per generated token, attention and the KV cache are untouched, and prefill is run either once or, optionally, twice for better performance. The obstacle is training. A pretrained model has never seen hidden states in its input, so latent feedback cannot simply be switched on at inference; and the recurrence it defines is sequential over positions, so training on it directly would forfeit the parallel teacher forcing that makes transformers efficient to train. We resolve this with a multi-pass regime (Sec. 3.3): each pass shifts the previous pass’s hidden states one position rightward, fuses them with the token embeddings, and re-runs the stack in parallel across all positions, so sequentiality is paid across a handful of passes rather than across the sequence. Two ingredients make this practical. A progressive schedule spends the bulk of training on the ordinary single-pass objective such that the run can start from a standard pretraining checkpoint and introduces extra feedback passes only late; and a prefix mixin randomizes where fused inputs begin within a sequence, matching the prompt-then-generate structure of inference. Empirically, we find the schedule’s composition matters in an unexpected way: training with two feedback passes alone produces a recurrence that diverges once rolled past its trained depth, whereas mixing in as little as 3% three-pass batches turns the learned map into a contraction toward a fixed point that stays stable beyond the trained depth (Fig. 3). Empirically, full-bandwidth transformers convert negligible extra inference compute into gains equivalent to substantially more training data. Utilizing multiple forward pass for prefill, the recurrence-trained model matches no-recurrence baselines trained on twice the tokens in both validation loss and multiple-choice accuracy (Fig. 4). On free-form generation (Fig. 5)—GSM8K, Math500, HumanEval, MBPP—latent feedback improves over standard decoding of the same weights on every task, matches the 2×-token baselines, and on some tasks approaches baselines trained with up to 5× the tokens; the gains carry over through long-context extension and instruction tuning (Table 1). On base models, latent feedback often yields markedly shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy (Fig. 6 and 8)—the behavior the widened channel predicts, with computation riding the hidden state instead of being verbalized token by token. 2 Full-bandwidth transformer 2 Background Given a vocabulary of size |V | and a D-dimensional residual stream, a decoder-only LLM maps an input sequence of T tokens, with embeddings {e t } T t=1 ∈ R T ×D , through L attention–MLP blocks. The final-layer hidden states {h L t } T t=1 are projected by the language-model head W head ∈ R |V |×D to next-token distributions: h L t = f θ (e t ; C), e t ← Decode ( h L t−1 ) , C = e 0 , e 1 , . . . , e t−1 . (1) KV cache. During autoregressive decoding with transformers, previously computed keys and values are cached and reused, avoiding repeated computation over the prefix. Unlike RNNs and state-space models, which compress history into a fixed-size recurrent state, dense-attention transformers retain explicit representations of all past tokens, so each new hidden state can attend directly to the full cached history. Bandwidths of a model’s horizonal axis vs. veritical axis. It is useful to separate the horizontal axis (across positions) from the vertical axis (across depth), because the two carry information at different rates. Horizontally, dense attention is effectively full-bandwidth: when generating token t, the layer-ℓ state h ℓ t can read the cached representations of every earlier position. Vertically, access is restricted: h ℓ t cannot read any deeper past state h ℓ ′ t ′ with t ′ < t and ℓ ′ ≥ ℓ (Fig. 1, left). Formally, the states reachable when computing position t at layer ℓ are R std (t, ℓ) = { (t ′ , ℓ ′ ) : t ′ < t, ℓ ′ < ℓ } , ∣ ∣ R std ∣ ∣ = Θ(T ℓ), (2) so a shallow layer of a new token sees only a partially processed view of the past, even though the deeper, more fully processed states of those same positions have already been computed and sit in the cache. Past computation therefore persists but is depth-frozen in that the representations produced at layer ℓ is readable only to layers above ℓ and can never be routed back down for further processing. This is the narrow vertical channel that sec. 3.1 widens. Importantly, this depth-wise dependency constraint is also what lets transformers train in parallel across positions: sequential computation is required only across layers, not across tokens. At decoding time, however, generation is already sequential over tokens, so the constraint buys nothing—opening the door to richer dependencies on past hidden states, which we develop next. 3 Widening the bandwidth with latent feedback decoding 3.1 Latent feedback decoding The central innovation in full-bandwidth transformer is latent feedback decoding, which feeds the previous top-layer hidden state back into the input. At step t, h L t = f θ ( e t ⊗ h L t−1 ; C ) , where e t ← Decode ( W head h L t−1 ) , C = e 0 , e 1 ⊗ h L 0 , . . . , e t−1 ⊗ h L t−2 (3) where f θ is the L-layer transformer stack, · ⊗ · fuses the sampled token’s embedding with the previous latent state, and C is the past context (the KV cache of all earlier positions). Standard decoding (Eq. (1)) is the special case in which only the sampled token crosses between steps. The fusion ⊗ is a gated linear unit: e t ⊗ h t−1 = W U h t−1 ⊙ σ(W G e t ), (4) with W U , W G ∈ R D×D . The asymmetry is deliberate: the hidden state occupies the value pathway, while the token embedding enters only as a multiplicative gate. A symmetric fusion such as e t + W h t−1 would leave a shortcut open: the model could suppress the state pathway, recover the plain token input, and reach ordinary pretraining loss, leaving the wide channel unused. That shortcut is especially tempting when training starts from a standard checkpoint whose low loss the additive path can reproduce. Eq. (4) closes it, since discarding h t−1 discards the input itself, and the token’s identity survives only in the D-dimensional gating pattern it imposes on the state. Reading the state is thereby mandatory rather than optional. Latent feedback is free to serve. The added inference cost is independent of context-length and model-depth and under 1% per token. The state h L t−1 is already computed during standard decoding, so the only extra work is the fusion: two D × D matrix multiplications, negligible against a forward pass through L blocks. Because fusion preserves the input dimension D, the architecture, KV-cache layout, and serving stack are untouched, and the decoding loop changes by two lines (Fig. 2, right). The scheme is also vLLM-compatible: we store top-layer states in a dedicated buffer, adapting the mechanism used by multi-token-prediction implementations (Appendix D). 3 Full-bandwidth transformer 3.2 Latent feedback decoding vs. standard CoT Standard CoT performs serial computation through a single feedback channel: each token is appended to the context and becomes the next input. The state is the token sequence, s t+1 = s t ∥a t , a t ∼ π θ (· | s t ) ∈ V, s t = x 1:t , (5) so the only thing crossing between steps is the discrete action sequence. The underlying problem-solving state may in principle be a deterministic function of the past actions, but recovering it from the token history is itself a state-tracking problem, and a fixed-depth transformer has only bounded serial computation per forward pass. CoT sidesteps this by externalizing intermediate state into language: the model writes out partial results, subgoals, and bookkeeping, then conditions future computation on the written trace. Let u i = e(a i−1 ) ⊗ z i−1 be the fused input at position i (with u 1 = e 0 ), so the attended context is C t = u 1:t−1 . The state is s t = (a 1:t , z t ): the token trace and the most recent latent. One step for latent feedback decoding is a t ∼ π θ (· | s t ) ∈ V, z t+1 = f θ (e(a t ) ⊗ z t ; u 1:t ) , a 1:t+1 = a 1:t ∥a t , (6) where · ⊗ · is the gate of Eq. (4) and f θ the full stack. The past latents z 1:t−1 are not carried explicitly: each is already folded into u 1:t and hence into the KV cache, so only z t , which the cache never stores, propagates as a recurrence variable. Latent feedback improves computational accessibility. Since z t+1 is a deterministic function of x 1:t+1 , it carries no information the context does not already determine; the gain is computational, not informational. Concretely, re-injection lifts the depth restriction of Eq. (2), whose reachable set requires ℓ ′ < ℓ, so that every layer, including the lowest, reads the full history, R lf (t, ℓ) = { (t ′ , ℓ ′ ) : t ′ < t, 0 ≤ ℓ ′ ≤ L } , ∣ ∣ R lf ∣ ∣ = Θ(T L), (7) shown in Fig. 1 (right). In standard CoT each new token instead accesses only a partially processed view of the context. The improved accessibility is also empirically verified in Sec. 4.4. Latent feedback adds draft space. Latent feedback also supplies an implicit scratchpad, relieving the pressure to verbalize intermediate state. State maintenance moves from the sequence axis alone to the depth axis as well: intermediate results can be updated through z along the stack rather than only by extending the token sequence. This predicts shorter rollouts on reasoning tasks, which Sec. 4.3 confirms. What latent feedback does not provide. We provide two important clarifications: • No mutable register. RNNs and state-space models overwrite a compressed state at each step. Latent feedback is recurrent in form, but past states persist in the KV cache rather than being overwritten, so every earlier state stays directly readable by the current token. • No added asymptotic depth at decoding time. Latent feedback does not change the serial depth of decoding: with or without it, each step has a depth-O(L) graph, so T tokens cost O(T L). What changes is the bandwidth of the path, with a verbal channel and a continuous channel now evolving in parallel. Note that a full-bandwidth transformer can further increase the depth at prefilling time through a multipass prefill, which we will introduce in the following section. 3.3 Parallel training for latent feedback decoding At decoding time, latent feedback unrolls over generated positions. We refer to this training scheme as temporal parallelism, following a common strategy for parallelizing recurrent computation during training (Zeng et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). Each pass is a Jacobi-style update of the latent-feedback recurrence: the hidden states from the previous pass are shifted one position to the right, fused with the token embeddings, and used to update all positions in parallel. Each additional pass therefore advances latent feedback by one token. After k passes, a top-layer state from position t can affect the input at positions up to t + k − 1, so k passes train the feedback transition over a horizon of k − 1 token steps. Training thus pays sequentiality across passes rather than across positions, reducing a length-T recurrent unroll to k parallel transformer evaluations, at roughly k× the compute of standard teacher forcing. The learned local transition is nevertheless the same one used during decoding, where latent feedback is applied causally once per generated token. Feedback-pass scheduling. At decoding time the feedback loop unrolls indefinitely, so the trained map must remain stable under many more self-compositions than any training budget can simulate; yet running many passes throughout training is prohibitively expensive, since each pass multiplies the cost of the run. Scheduling the number of forward passes—how many, and when—is therefore central to making latent-feedback training practical. How many passes. We choose the number of passes by checking whether the iterated feedback map reaches a stable fixed point: a depth beyond which additional passes neither change the hidden states substantially nor improve the loss. This stability is easier to obtain than in architectures that repeatedly recompute the entire input (e.g. a loop transformer), because each feedback pass keeps the token embedding fixed and updates only the hidden-state pathway through the gate. In practice, this means the goal is not to train at the full inference horizon, but to train the feedback map until it becomes stable under further self-composition. When to introduce feedback passes. Because feedback passes are expensive, most of training uses the standard single-pass objective. We introduce latent feedback progressively in the middle of training: first with two-pass batches, and later with a small fraction of batches with more passes. This lets the run begin from an ordinary pretrained checkpoint, spend the bulk of its compute on standard teacher forcing, and pay the extra feedback-pass cost only mid-training, when it is needed to stabilize the feedback map. Fig. 3 illustrates the feasibility of the scheduling. We studied a 1B model trained on 200B tokens. A model trained with only single- and two-pass batches (75% single-pass, 25% two-pass; green) performs well at the trained depth but fails to extrapolate: beyond that depth, validation loss rises sharply and the hidden-state change ∥h (k) − h (k−1) ∥ oscillates rather than decays, indicating that the iterates have left the trained state distribution. Adding only 3% three-pass batches (75% single-pass, 22% two-pass, 3% three-pass; blue) qualitatively changes the behavior: validation loss remains flat through 30 feedback steps, and the hidden-state change decays to a small plateau. This suggests that the learned feedback map behaves like a contraction toward a fixed point, making feedback depths far beyond those seen in training stable in our tests. The same extrapolation behavior carries over to inference: hundred-token rollouts show no sign of breakdown (Fig. 5, solid green line), and we observe similar stability under k = 1000 feedback passes (Fig. 10 in the appendix). Prefix mixin. A distribution mismatch remains between multi-pass training and inference. At decoding time a sequence is heterogeneous: prompt positions carry plain token embeddings (processed by a single prefill pass), while generated positions carry fused inputs. In the passes of Eqs. (10)–(11), by contrast, every position beyond the first is fused. A model trained only on fully-fused passes therefore encounters an out-of-distribution boundary at inference, precisely where the prompt ends and generation begins. To close this gap we apply a prefix mixin: in each pass beyond the first, we sample a random prefix length p and revert positions t ≤ p to plain embeddings, fusing only the suffix. Training thus covers sequences that switch from plain to fused inputs at an arbitrary point, i.e. the structure of single-prefill inference. Alternatively, the prompt itself can be run through a second, fused prefill pass so that all positions match the fused distribution; the mixin removes the need for this, but we support both, corresponding to the “identical or doubled prefill” overhead stated in the abstract. 6 Full-bandwidth transformer Stability recipes for long feedback horizons. At inference time, latent feedback may be applied for hundreds or thousands of generated tokens, far beyond the few feedback passes used during training. We therefore use several lightweight stabilization techniques to keep the feedback map well behaved under long self-composition. • Stationary hidden-state scale. We keep the magnitude of carried state h L t bounded as feedback is repeatedly applied. To prevent the top-layer state norm from growing with depth, we use depth scaling (Yang et al., 2024; Noci et al., 2022) so that ∥ ∥ h L t ∥ ∥ ∼ O(1) rather than O(L), as can occur in a standard pre-norm model. We also apply RMSNorm to the fused input e t ⊗ h L t−1 before feeding it into the model. • Shared input basis with weight tying. The model processes two types of inputs: plain token embeddings during standard prefill, and fused hidden-state/token inputs during latent-feedback decoding. We therefore encourage the embedding space and top-layer hidden-state space to remain in a compatible basis by tying the weights of the embedding layer and readout layer, reducing the burden on the fusion weights to learn a large corrective rotation between the two input distributions. • Noise regularization. During training, we add small jitter noise to the carried hidden state before fusion, h L t = f θ ( e t ⊗ h L t−1 + ϵ; C ) , ϵ ∼ Uniform[−σ, σ] D . (13) This exposes the feedback map to a local neighborhood around each training state, making it less sensitive to small deviations that can accumulate over long feedback horizons. The complete pseudo code for training where the tricks are adopted is presented in Fig. 9 in the appendix. 3.4 Latent-feedback training improves pre-training data efficiency Beyond enabling latent feedback at decoding time, the feedback passes also act as an auxiliary training signal on the hidden states. In the standard next-token-prediction loss, the top-layer state h L t is supervised only through the prediction of the next token. In later feedback passes, however, h L t is shifted, fused into the input of subsequent positions, and can influence losses at multiple future positions through causal attention. Thus gradients from later predictions backpropagate into earlier hidden states, encouraging them to be reusable as inputs rather than merely predictive at the output layer. Empirically, this improves pre-training data efficiency even when latent feedback is not used at decoding time. When evaluated with standard decoding, models trained with the latent-feedback objective improve on LM Eval and free-form generation tasks relative to comparable models trained only with the ordinary next-token objective. We can therefore view latent-feedback training as a way to spend additional training-time compute on the same token stream, improving the representations without changing the serving-time decoding pipeline. Latent-feedback training also enables a simple form of prefill-time test-time scaling. At evaluation, we can apply k additional fused passes over the prompt using Eqs. (10)–(11). These passes refine the prompt states before generation begins, improving perplexity and downstream accuracy at the cost of k extra parallel prefill forward passes. The only per-token overhead is two D × D matrix multiplications. • FUSED: the prompt is first processed by an additional fused prefill pass, as in Eq. (10); generation then proceeds as in SOFT. This gives the prompt states one round of latent-feedback refinement before decoding begins, at the cost of one extra prefill pass that is parallel over prompt tokens. Thus STANDARD and SOFT have identical prefill cost, while FUSED doubles prefill cost while keeping the same per-token decoding cost as SOFT and effectively STANDARD. Evaluation setting. This is the behavior the widened channel predicts: intermediate computation that STANDARD must verbalize—token by token, at log 2 |V | bits per step—can instead ride the hidden state, so fewer tokens are needed to reach the answer. Notably, the effect disappears after instruction tuning. We attribute this to the tuning data being off-policy with respect to latent-feedback decoding: the target traces were produced by (and imitate the verbosity of) standard token-by-token reasoning, so fitting them re-imposes the fully verbalized style regardless of what the state can carry. On-policy post-training under latent feedback may preserve the conciseness, which we leave to future work 4.4 Full-bandwidth transformer carries richer information in shallow-layer residuals Lastly, to verify the added bandwidth directly, we run controlled state-tracking experiments in which the target is fixed but the intervening context varies (full construction in App. F). Two tasks isolate the effect. Completion tracking asks whether a completed counter has reached a required one after a run of no-op updates; delayed memory asks the model to recover an initial binary state after a sequence of label-independent scratch operations. Both end at a shared colon, and the label is determined entirely by information before it, so a probe at that colon measures how much of the global state each layer has already reconstructed. Under standard prefilling, the final token enters as its plain embedding; under one-step recurrent prefilling, that embedding is fused with the preceding token’s top-layer state (Eq. One central idea behind full bandwidth transformer is to introduce extra compute that overlaps with the sequential decoding process. There are other works that consider similar ideas. Feedback Transformer (Fan et al., 2020) is the pioneering work along this line; At each position, they generate a mixture of each layer’s representation and let attention in future positions attend to aggregated representation rather than the same-layer key values as in standard transformers. However, their training is sequential over input tokens, limiting their scalability, whereas our training is parallelized over all positions. Additionally, our approach does not involve modifying the structure but only the input. Note that their ablations also support our choice of feedback layer: a memory built from the topmost layer alone nearly matches the full-layer mixture, 11 Full-bandwidth transformer Problem What is the last nonzero digit to the right of the decimal point in the decimal expansion of 137 500 ?
